vignette: Lani had always been a pillar of strength for her family and friends. As a project manager in her early sixties, she was known for her sharp mind and warm demeanor. But when she was diagnosed with a life-threatening illness two years ago, everything changed. The medical procedures that followed were grueling, and Lani couldn't shake off the feeling of vulnerability that lingered long after she had recovered. Simple things like getting a check-up or seeing medical equipment would send her heart racing, making her irritable and short-tempered with those around her. Her husband, normally her rock, found himself walking on eggshells around her, never knowing when a seemingly innocuous conversation might trigger an outburst. As she reflected on that difficult period, Lani realized that certain conversation topics - anything related to health or illness - would transport her back to the hospital room where she had received her diagnosis. She would feel her body tense up, as if she was reliving the experience all over again, with every sense on high alert. Her mind would struggle to put words to what had happened, leaving her feeling frustrated and ashamed. These episodes of full sensory reliving left Lani feeling like her life had been destroyed by the trauma. She couldn't trust her own body anymore, which in turn made her even more anxious about medical procedures or conversations that might trigger another episode. Her body would involuntarily take on the same position as when she was in the hospital bed, a constant reminder of her powerlessness. As time went on, Lani began to notice that these memories were not just triggered by external stimuli but also by her own thoughts and emotions. When she felt threatened or anxious, memories of her illness would flood back, making it difficult for her to concentrate or think clearly. She would startle at the slightest touch, as if her body was perpetually on guard. Lani's negative appraisals about her body and the trauma had created a self-reinforcing cycle. Her feelings of shame and mistrust towards her own body made her more prone to memories and triggers, which in turn reinforced those same negative appraisals. She felt trapped in this vicious loop, unable to escape the past. As she navigated her daily life as a project manager, Lani found it increasingly difficult to cope with the stress of her job. Her irritability and difficulty concentrating began to affect her relationships with colleagues and clients. It was only when she realized that she couldn't continue living like this - constantly on edge, unable to trust herself or her body - that Lani finally sought help. Now, as she begins therapy, Lani is hoping to break free from the grip of her trauma. She wants to learn how to manage her triggers and memories, to find a way to reconcile with her past and rebuild her sense of self-trust. But for now, she remains fearful of what might happen if she can't - will she be forever trapped in this cycle of fear and anxiety?
